doctrines.question: What is baptism in the Holy Spirit, and when does it occur?
doctrines.framing: Every tradition agrees that Scripture speaks of believers being baptized in, filled with, or receiving the Holy Spirit. The disagreement is over whether this names a distinct, usually post-conversion experience to be sought, sometimes evidenced by tongues, or is simply Paul's own term for the Spirit's ordinary work of joining every believer to Christ and the church at conversion, a work some traditions locate sacramentally in confirmation or chrismation.
doctrines.tier_note: Thomas's own map places this between the second and third tier: it shapes expectation and practice sharply without dividing on the gospel itself.

open.todo: Work out whether baptism in the Holy Spirit names a second, post-conversion experience or is simply Paul's term for the Spirit's work of joining a believer to Christ at conversion, and if it is a second experience, whether tongues is its necessary sign.

positions.label: Subsequent with tongues
positions.hold: Baptism in the Holy Spirit is a distinct experience subsequent to conversion, given to empower witness and evidenced initially by speaking in other tongues as the Spirit gives utterance.
positions.why: Acts repeatedly narrates believers already converted subsequently receiving the Spirit with power, accompanied by tongues as the consistent, repeated sign of that reception.
positions.vs: Treating the reception of the Spirit that empowers witness as identical with, and exhausted by, the Spirit's work of regeneration at conversion.
positions.orthodoxy_note:
Disputed: Whether a Christian receives the Spirit fully at conversion, or later has a separate experience called baptism in the Holy Spirit, first shown by speaking in tongues.
Who: Pentecostal churches such as the Assemblies of God teach the separate experience; Reformed, Baptist, Lutheran and many non-denominational churches say every believer receives the Spirit at conversion.
At stake: Whether Christians should seek a further experience of the Spirit.

held_by.note: The statement says: "This experience is distinct from and subsequent to the experience of the new birth" (Article 7, The Baptism in the Holy Spirit).
held_by.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 7

positions.learn_detail: Classical Pentecostalism distinguishes this experience sharply from conversion: a believer is regenerate and indwelt by the Spirit at conversion, then subsequently baptized in the Spirit for power in witness.

sources.label: Assemblies of God Statement of Fundamental Truths

positions.label: Second blessing
positions.hold: Baptism in the Holy Spirit is a second, definite work of grace subsequent to conversion, in which the believer is entirely sanctified and filled with perfect love.
positions.why: Wesley taught a second work of grace beyond justification in which the believer is cleansed from inbred sin, and the nineteenth-century holiness movement applied the term baptism in the Holy Spirit to that experience.
positions.vs: Collapsing sanctification into a single, gradual process beginning and ending with conversion, with no further definite crisis experience to seek.
positions.orthodoxy_note:
Disputed: Whether a believer can have one definite experience after conversion, called baptism in the Holy Spirit by some, that makes them entirely loving and free from sin in this life.
Who: Holiness churches in the Methodist tradition teach it; Reformed and other Protestant churches say holiness grows gradually and is never complete in this life. Pentecostals use the phrase differently.
At stake: Whether to seek a moment of complete holiness or expect slow growth.

held_by.note: A holiness-movement development of Wesley's own doctrine of entire sanctification; the term baptism in the Holy Spirit for this experience postdates Wesley and is held now mainly within the holiness wing of the Wesleyan family rather than mainstream contemporary Methodism.
held_by.citation: John Wesley, A Plain Account of Christian Perfection (1777)

positions.learn_detail: The holiness movement, through figures such as Phoebe Palmer, renamed Wesley's second work of grace as baptism in the Holy Spirit; classical Pentecostalism inherited this vocabulary from the holiness movement before redefining the experience around power for witness rather than entire sanctification.

sources.label: A Plain Account of Christian Perfection

positions.label: Conversion-initiation
positions.hold: Baptism in the Holy Spirit is Paul's term for the Spirit's work of uniting every believer to Christ and to the church at conversion, not a second or separate experience to be sought afterward.
positions.why: Paul writes that all the Corinthian believers, without exception, were baptized by one Spirit into one body, using the same language Acts uses for a converting, initiating work of the Spirit.
positions.vs: Treating the same baptism in one Spirit that Paul says every believer already has as a further experience still to be sought after conversion.

held_by.note: Not confessionally addressed by name, but consistent with the Book of Concord's treatment of the Spirit's work as a single, unified act of grace rather than staged experiences.
held_by.citation: Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration, Article II

sources.label: Baptism and Fullness

positions.label: Sacramental initiation
positions.hold: The fullness of the Holy Spirit given at conversion is sealed and completed in the sacrament of confirmation, or chrismation, administered through the laying on of hands and anointing with chrism.
positions.why: The apostles laid hands on the newly baptized so that they might receive the Holy Spirit, and the church continues this apostolic act as the sacrament that completes Christian initiation begun in baptism.
positions.vs: Locating the giving of the Spirit's fullness in an inward experience sought apart from the church's sacramental rite of confirmation or chrismation.

held_by.note: Q307: “Unction with Chrism is a Sacrament, in which the baptized believer, being anointed with holy chrism ... in the name of the Holy Ghost, receives the gifts of the Holy Ghost for growth and strength in spiritual life.” The previous citation named the Catechism with no question number.
held_by.citation: Longer Catechism of St Philaret of Moscow, Qq. 307-310 (On Unction with Chrism)

sources.label: Catechism of the Catholic Church

doctrines.learn_note:
Key terms: baptism in the Holy Spirit — a New Testament phrase for receiving the Spirit, used differently by churches; second blessing — a definite experience after conversion; entire sanctification — being made fully loving and free from deliberate sin in this life.
How it developed: In the 1700s John Wesley taught a second work of grace. By the 1800s holiness preachers such as Phoebe Palmer called it baptism in the Holy Spirit. Pentecostals, from the Azusa Street revival (Los Angeles, 1906), kept the phrase but tied it to power for witness and speaking in tongues.

sources.label: Perspectives on Spirit Baptism: Five Views

doctrines.question: When and how does the sealing of the Holy Spirit named in Ephesians take place?
doctrines.framing: Paul writes that believers are sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, a guarantee of their inheritance. The disagreement is over whether this seal is simply the Spirit himself, given the moment a person believes the gospel, or is sacramentally sealed and made visible in confirmation or chrismation, the rite the church connects to the apostolic laying on of hands.
doctrines.tier_note: Thomas's own map places this at the second tier: it bears on assurance and church practice without dividing on the gospel itself.

open.todo: Work out whether sealing happens at conversion as another name for the Spirit's indwelling, or is completed in a later sacramental act such as chrismation or confirmation.

positions.label: Sealed at conversion
positions.hold: The sealing of the Holy Spirit named in Ephesians occurs at the moment of believing, when the Spirit himself is given as God's mark of ownership and down payment guaranteeing the believer's inheritance.
positions.why: Paul locates the seal at the moment of hearing and believing the gospel, identifying the seal with the gift of the Spirit himself rather than with any later rite or experience.
positions.vs: Locating the completion of the Spirit's seal in a later sacramental act rather than in the Spirit's own gift at the moment of faith.

held_by.citation: Wesley's Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (1755), on Ephesians 1:13

sources.label: The Holy Spirit

positions.label: Sacramental sealing
positions.hold: The Spirit's seal named in Ephesians is sacramentally sealed and made visible in confirmation, or chrismation, when the newly baptized are anointed and receive the gift of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands.
positions.why: The apostles laid hands on the newly baptized to give the Spirit, and the church's rite of confirmation or chrismation continues that apostolic act as the visible completion of the seal Scripture describes.
positions.vs: Treating the Spirit's seal as complete in an inward, unmediated gift at the moment of believing, without the church's sacramental act connected to the laying on of hands.

held_by.note: The Catechism itself uses the language of seal for this sacrament.
The chrismation rite's own formula names the gift a seal.
held_by.citation: Orthodox chrismation rite: 'The seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit'

sources.label: Catechism of the Catholic Church

doctrines.learn_note:
Key terms: seal — in Ephesians, a guarantee of God's promise; chrismation — in Orthodox churches, anointing a newly baptized person with oil, said to give the Spirit's seal; confirmation — the Catholic rite where a baptized person is anointed with oil and receives the Spirit in fullness.
How it developed: Ephesians 1:13 says believers are sealed with the Spirit. From the early centuries the church linked this to anointing and laying on of hands after baptism. Many Protestants read the seal as the Spirit himself, given when a person first believes.

sources.label: The Holy Spirit

doctrines.question: Do the miraculous spiritual gifts described in the New Testament continue in the church today?
doctrines.framing: Every tradition agrees that the New Testament describes tongues, prophecy, healing and other miraculous gifts operating in the apostolic church. The disagreement is over whether those gifts were tied to the foundational apostolic era and its accompanying sign of Scripture-authenticating revelation, or continue as an ordinary part of the Spirit's work in the church until Christ returns.
doctrines.tier_note: Thomas's own map places continuationism at the second tier: it shapes how a congregation worships and what it expects of the Spirit, without dividing on the gospel itself.

open.todo: Work out whether 'the perfect' in 1 Corinthians 13:10 refers to the completed canon, the return of Christ, or something else, and decide whether Acts' pattern of ongoing tongues and prophecy is descriptive of an apostolic season or a standing norm.

positions.label: Cessationist
positions.hold: The revelatory and sign gifts, including tongues, prophecy and the working of miracles as attesting apostolic ministry, ceased with the apostolic era and the completion of the New Testament canon.
positions.why: The sign gifts served to authenticate the apostles' foundational message before Scripture was complete, and the New Testament itself anticipates their passing once what is perfect, understood as the completed revelation, has come.
positions.vs: Continuing the full range of New Testament spiritual gifts as an ordinary part of church life today.

held_by.note: Not confessionally required by the Westminster Standards themselves, but the predominant position among Reformed and Presbyterian bodies since the modern cessationist-continuationist debate emerged.
Widely but not universally held; the Baptist Faith and Message does not itself settle the question.
held_by.citation: John MacArthur, Charismatic Chaos (1992), representative of a major strand of Baptist cessationism

positions.learn_detail: Cessationism is a position about the sign and revelatory gifts specifically; cessationists typically still affirm that God heals and answers prayer, distinguishing ordinary providence from the apostolic sign gifts.

sources.label: Counterfeit Miracles

positions.label: Continuationist
positions.hold: The spiritual gifts described in 1 Corinthians 12, including tongues, prophecy and healing, continue to be given by the Holy Spirit to the church today and are to be earnestly desired.
positions.why: Paul commands the Corinthian church to desire spiritual gifts and gives no indication that they would cease before Christ's return, and 'the perfect' of 1 Corinthians 13:10 is most naturally the eschaton rather than the closing of the canon.
positions.vs: Restricting the sign and revelatory gifts to the apostolic era before the completion of the New Testament canon.

held_by.note: The statement says the baptism in the Holy Spirit brings "the bestowment of the gifts and their uses in the work of the ministry" (Article 7), and that speaking in tongues "is the same in essence as the gift of tongues" (Article 8) — both treating the New Testament gifts as continuing.
held_by.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 7-8

held_by.note: The statement says: “All of the spiritual gifts as outlined in 1 Corinthians 12:8-10 are still in operation and are available to believers for the building up of the church and for the glory of God.”
held_by.citation: International Network of Churches, Statement of Faith (Declaration of Faith, February 2022), "The Baptism and Gifts of The Holy Spirit"

held_by.note: Affirmed through the Catholic Charismatic Renewal, recognised by Rome, alongside a broader church that does not emphasise the gifts.
Held within the charismatic wing of the Communion; not a position the Articles themselves address.
held_by.citation: Church of England, House of Bishops, statements recognising charismatic renewal within the Communion

positions.learn_detail: Continuationists divide further on how the gifts are exercised in practice, from classical Pentecostal expectation of tongues as initial evidence of Spirit baptism to a lighter charismatic openness within otherwise traditional worship.

sources.label: Are Miraculous Gifts for Today? Four Views
International Network of Churches, Declaration of Faith
sources.citation: February 2022, "The Baptism and Gifts of The Holy Spirit"

sources.label: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths

doctrines.learn_note:
Key terms: spiritual gifts — abilities the Spirit gives believers, such as tongues, prophecy and healing; cessationist — holds that the miraculous gifts ended with the apostles; continuationist — holds that they still operate today.
How it developed: The question grew sharp after Pentecostalism began in the early 1900s. B. B. Warfield's Counterfeit Miracles (1918) is a classic argument that the gifts ended. From the 1960s charismatic renewal brought the gifts into older churches too.
Common mix-up: Both sides believe God still heals and answers prayer.

sources.label: Are Miraculous Gifts for Today? Four Views

doctrines.question: Does prophecy, as a Spirit-given gift of speaking God's word, operate in the church today?
doctrines.framing: The New Testament describes prophecy as a gift exercised in the earliest congregations, tested and weighed by the church. The disagreement is over whether prophecy is a single, canon-forming category that necessarily ceased once the New Testament was complete, or whether congregational prophecy today is a genuine but fallible, weighable gift distinct from the Scripture-forming prophecy of the prophets and apostles.
doctrines.tier_note: Thomas's own map places prophecy at the second tier: it shapes worship and expectation of the Spirit without dividing on the gospel itself.

open.todo: Work out whether New Testament congregational prophecy is a lesser, fallible category distinct from Scripture-forming prophecy, or whether prophecy is a single category that necessarily ceased when the canon closed.

positions.label: Cessationist
positions.hold: The revelatory gift of prophecy, understood as the Spirit speaking fresh words through a human messenger, ceased with the closing of the New Testament canon; the church's ongoing task is the faithful preaching and application of the completed Scriptures.
positions.why: Prophecy belonged to the foundation-laying office of apostles and prophets, and once that foundation, the New Testament, was complete, the office that produced it had accomplished its purpose.
positions.vs: Continuing to receive a category of Spirit-prompted prophetic speech alongside the completed canon of Scripture.

held_by.note: Widely but not universally held.

sources.label: Counterfeit Miracles

positions.label: Fallible congregational
positions.hold: The gift of prophecy in the local congregation today is a Spirit-prompted impression that a believer reports in their own words; it is not equal to Scripture in authority, and the congregation must weigh it, testing all things and holding fast to what is good.
positions.why: Paul commands the Corinthian congregation to weigh what is prophesied rather than simply receive it, an instruction that would be needless if congregational prophecy carried Scripture's own unquestionable authority.
positions.vs: Treating New Testament congregational prophecy as carrying the same unweighable authority as the prophetic word that produced Scripture, so that it necessarily ceased once the canon closed.
positions.orthodoxy_note:
Disputed: Whether Christians today can give prophecy that is a real gift from the Spirit but may contain mistakes and must be tested against Scripture.
Who: Many non-denominational churches and charismatic Anglicans say yes; Reformed and Baptist cessationists say prophecy ended with the New Testament, and some charismatics reject fallible prophecy.
At stake: Whether churches should expect messages from God, and how much weight they carry.

held_by.citation: Wayne Grudem, The Gift of Prophecy in the New Testament and Today (1988)

held_by.note: Held within the charismatic wing of the Communion.
held_by.citation: Church of England, House of Bishops, statements recognising charismatic renewal within the Communion

sources.label: The Gift of Prophecy in the New Testament and Today

positions.label: Canonical authority
positions.hold: True prophecy carries the same Spirit-breathed, unweighable authority as Old Testament prophecy; there is no lesser, fallible category of prophetic speech, so the gift that produced authoritative revelation ceased once the canon it was producing was complete.
positions.why: Scripture nowhere distinguishes a fallible congregational prophecy from the prophecy that produced its own text, so treating New Testament prophecy as a lesser category reads a modern distinction back into the text.
positions.vs: Dividing prophecy into a canon-forming, infallible kind that has ceased and a congregational, fallible kind that continues, when Scripture presents prophecy as a single category.
positions.learn_detail: This is a specific argument within cessationism, distinct from the general appeal to the closing of the canon: it denies that a fallible, lesser category of prophecy can be coherently derived from Scripture at all.

sources.label: The Final Word: A Biblical Response to the Case for Tongues and Prophecy Today

doctrines.learn_note:
Key terms: prophecy — in the New Testament, a message a believer says the Spirit prompted; canon — the list of books accepted as Scripture; fallible — able to contain mistakes; cessationist — holds that prophecy ended with the New Testament.
How it developed: The New Testament shows prophets in the early churches, and Paul tells the Corinthians to weigh what is said (1 Corinthians 14:29). The question grew sharper as Pentecostal and charismatic churches spread in the 1900s. Wayne Grudem's 1988 book argued for fallible congregational prophecy.

sources.label: Are Miraculous Gifts for Today? Four Views

doctrines.question: Does speaking in tongues, as described in Acts and 1 Corinthians, operate in the church today, and what is its significance?
doctrines.framing: Acts and 1 Corinthians both describe believers speaking in tongues under the Spirit's prompting. The disagreement is over whether tongues is the necessary initial evidence of a distinct baptism in the Holy Spirit, one gift among several the Spirit distributes to some believers and not others, or a sign gift tied to the apostolic era that ceased with the completion of the New Testament canon.
doctrines.tier_note: Thomas's own map places tongues at the second tier: it shapes worship practice and expectation without dividing on the gospel itself.

open.todo: Work out whether speaking in tongues is the necessary evidence of a distinct baptism in the Holy Spirit, one gift among several given to some believers, or a sign gift that ceased with the apostolic era.

positions.label: Initial evidence
positions.hold: Speaking in other tongues is the initial physical evidence that a believer has been baptized in the Holy Spirit, the outward sign that regularly accompanied that experience throughout the book of Acts.
positions.why: In every full narrative of believers receiving the Spirit's baptism recorded in Acts, tongues is what results, establishing a consistent pattern rather than a coincidence.
positions.vs: Treating tongues as one gift among several, distributed to some believers and not others, rather than as the expected sign of an experience available to every Spirit-baptized believer.
positions.orthodoxy_note:
Disputed: Whether tongues is the sign every Spirit-baptized believer will show, or only one gift the Spirit gives to some.
Who: Pentecostal churches such as the Assemblies of God teach it is the first sign; Catholic, Anglican and many non-denominational charismatics call it one gift among several, and cessationists say it ended with the apostles.
At stake: Whether someone who has never spoken in tongues is missing what the Spirit offers every Christian.

held_by.note: The statement says: "The baptism of believers in the Holy Spirit is witnessed by the initial physical sign of speaking with other tongues as the Spirit of God gives them utterance" (Article 8, The Initial Physical Evidence of the Baptism in the Holy Spirit — not Article 7, which is the baptism itself).
held_by.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 8

sources.label: Assemblies of God Statement of Fundamental Truths

positions.label: Gift to some
positions.hold: Tongues is one spiritual gift among several that the Spirit distributes to believers as he chooses, not a necessary sign given to every believer or evidence of a separate baptism in the Spirit.
positions.why: Paul asks rhetorically whether all speak in tongues, expecting the answer no, placing tongues alongside the other gifts the Spirit apportions to each individually as he wills.
positions.vs: Requiring tongues as the necessary evidence of Spirit baptism for every believer, rather than treating it as one gift given to some.

held_by.note: Broader charismatic streams within the Pentecostal-charismatic movement, distinct from classical Pentecostal denominations; see the tradition override below.

The Catechism says: "There are furthermore special graces, also called charisms... Whatever their character — sometimes it is extraordinary, such as the gift of miracles or of tongues... charisms are oriented toward sanctifying grace and are intended for the common good of the Church."
Held within the charismatic wing of the Communion.
held_by.citation: Church of England, House of Bishops, statements recognising charismatic renewal within the Communion

sources.label: Power Evangelism
Catechism of the Catholic Church

positions.label: Cessationist
positions.hold: Tongues, understood as a Spirit-given sign gift authenticating apostolic revelation, ceased with the completion of the New Testament canon and is not to be sought or expected today.
positions.why: Tongues functioned in Acts and 1 Corinthians as a sign gift tied to the apostolic, revelation-giving era, and Scripture anticipates its passing once what is perfect, the completed revelation, has come.
positions.vs: Continuing to seek or practise tongues as an ordinary part of church life after the apostolic era and the closing of the canon.

held_by.note: Widely but not universally held.

sources.label: Counterfeit Miracles

doctrines.learn_note:
Key terms: tongues — speaking in words the speaker has not learned, taken as Spirit-prompted; initial evidence — the view that tongues is the first sign of being baptized in the Spirit; cessationist — holds that tongues ended with the apostles.
How it developed: Acts 2 describes tongues at Pentecost, and Paul discusses them in 1 Corinthians 12–14. Modern Pentecostalism began in the early 1900s, with the Azusa Street revival (Los Angeles, 1906), and made tongues central. From the 1960s charismatic renewal spread tongues into Catholic and Anglican churches as one gift among several.

sources.label: Are Miraculous Gifts for Today? Four Views

pentecostal.hold: Classical Pentecostal denominations confessionally teach tongues as the necessary initial evidence of Spirit baptism; broader charismatic streams within the Pentecostal-charismatic movement hold tongues as one gift among several, not a required sign.
pentecostal.note: The movement is not unanimous: this is the one point where classical Pentecostal confession and the wider charismatic stream it gave rise to genuinely part ways.
pentecostal.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 8, contrasted with charismatic-stream teaching such as John Wimber, Power Evangelism (1985)

doctrines.question: Does the Holy Spirit heal the sick today, and if so, on what terms?
doctrines.framing: The New Testament describes both Jesus and the apostles healing the sick, and James instructs the elders to pray over the sick in faith. The disagreement is over whether physical healing is provided for in the atonement as the privilege of every believer to claim, a real gift God grants at his own sovereign discretion rather than as an entitlement, or a sign gift tied to the apostolic era that ceased with the closing of the canon.
doctrines.tier_note: Thomas's own map places healing at the second tier: it shapes expectation and pastoral practice without dividing on the gospel itself.

open.todo: Work out whether physical healing is guaranteed in this life through the atonement, a real gift given at God's sovereign discretion, or a sign gift that ceased with the apostolic era while God still heals providentially.

positions.label: In the atonement
positions.hold: Divine healing of the body is provided for in Christ's atonement alongside forgiveness of sins, and is the privilege of every believer to seek in faith as part of the full provision of the gospel.
positions.why: Isaiah's suffering servant bears both iniquities and sicknesses, and Matthew applies that same passage to Jesus's healing ministry, joining bodily healing to the atoning work that also secures forgiveness.
positions.vs: Separating physical healing entirely from the atonement and treating it as an unrelated act of ordinary providence rather than part of the gospel's full provision.
positions.orthodoxy_note:
Disputed: Whether Christ's death guarantees bodily healing in this life to every believer who asks in faith, as it does forgiveness.
Who: Pentecostal churches such as the Assemblies of God teach this; Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches pray for the sick but see healing as God's gift at his discretion; Reformed and Baptist cessationists say miraculous healing ended with the apostles.
At stake: Whether people who stay ill are made to feel their faith failed.

held_by.note: The statement says: "Divine healing is an integral part of the gospel. Deliverance from sickness is provided for in the Atonement, and is the privilege of all believers" (Article 12, Divine Healing).
held_by.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 12

sources.label: Assemblies of God Statement of Fundamental Truths

positions.label: Real but sovereign gift
positions.hold: God really heals the sick today in answer to believing prayer, but does so as a sovereign gift given according to his own will rather than as an entitlement guaranteed to every believer who asks in faith.
positions.why: James instructs the elders to pray over the sick and anoint them with oil, promising that the prayer of faith will save the sick, while the rest of the New Testament's healings remain acts of God's free compassion rather than a formula.
positions.vs: Guaranteeing physical healing in this life as a provision of the atonement that faith can claim, so that continued sickness is read as a failure of faith.

held_by.note: Affirmed through the Catholic Charismatic Renewal, alongside the sacrament of Anointing of the Sick.

Q364: “Unction with Oil is a Sacrament, in which, while the body is anointed with oil, God's grace is invoked on the sick, to heal him of spiritual and bodily infirmities.” The previous citation named the Catechism with no question number.
held_by.citation: Longer Catechism of St Philaret of Moscow, Qq. 364-365 (On Unction with Oil)
Book of Common Prayer (1662), Visitation of the Sick

sources.label: Catechism of the Catholic Church

positions.label: Cessationist
positions.hold: The charismatic gift of healing, understood as a Spirit-given sign gift authenticating apostolic ministry, ceased with the apostolic era; God still heals in answer to ordinary prayer and providence, but not through a standing gift of healing exercised by particular believers.
positions.why: Healing functioned in Acts as a sign accompanying apostolic preaching before the New Testament was complete, and the sign gifts belong to that foundational era rather than to the ongoing life of the church.
positions.vs: Treating healing as a standing charismatic gift exercised by particular believers today, rather than as God's ordinary providential response to prayer.

held_by.note: Widely but not universally held.

positions.learn_detail: Cessationists typically still affirm that God heals providentially through prayer and medicine, distinguishing this from a standing charismatic gift of healing exercised by particular believers.

sources.label: Counterfeit Miracles

doctrines.learn_note:
Key terms: atonement — Christ's death for sin; healing in the atonement — the belief that it also won bodily healing for every believer; anointing of the sick — praying over someone with oil,; cessationist — holds that miraculous healing ended with the apostles.
How it developed: James 5 tells church elders to pray over the sick, and Catholic and Orthodox churches keep anointing as a sacrament. In the late 1800s holiness leaders such as A. B. Simpson taught healing in the atonement; Pentecostal churches later wrote it into their statements of faith.

sources.label: Are Miraculous Gifts for Today? Four Views
